In European whitefish (Coregonus lavaretus), the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 16% [GSI = 16%], determined under controlled laboratory temperatures of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] in gravid females collected from oligotrophic lakes. This value aligns with reported indices for other coregonines, reflecting the relatively modest investment in ovarian tissue prior to spawning. Newly hatched alevins emerge from demersal eggs at an extremely small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a mass derived from the typical egg diameter of related species. This minute size at the yolk-sac larva stage necessitates a period of rapid endogenous feeding before the onset of exogenous feeding, during which the prolarvae rely entirely on their yolk reserves. The estimated mass of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] places Coregonus lavaretus among the smaller-bodied salmoniform neonates, consistent with its strategy of producing numerous, small offspring.

Populations of European whitefish display considerable plasticity in growth, yet field surveys indicate a consistent ultimate total length of 73 centimeters [Li = 73 centimeters], representing the asymptotic body size attained by the largest adults in most lacustrine systems. This maximum body length is typically reached after several years of feeding on zooplankton and benthic invertebrates, with growth rates modulated by local productivity and thermal regimes. In contrast, the length at which females first attain puberty is substantially lower, with a total length at puberty for females of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters]. This threshold marks the point at which vitellogenesis is initiated and ovarian recrudescence begins. The difference of nearly fifty centimeters between the size at maturity and the asymptotic length underscores a prolonged period of somatic growth following the onset of reproductive capability, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts.

Assessments of maximum longevity in Coregonus lavaretus, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith readings, support a life span of approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days] under the thermal conditions typical of boreal lakes, with a recorded temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This considerable lifespan, spanning roughly fifteen years, is characteristic of a K-selected life history strategy within the Salmonidae family. The ultimate wet weight attained by the oldest and largest individuals can reach 10000 grams [Wwi = 10000 grams], a mass representing the culmination of decades of feeding on available prey resources. This ultimate wet weight is among the highest recorded for lacustrine coregonines, with the heaviest adults often exceeding the size of their congeneric counterparts in more productive habitats.

Reproductive studies have clarified the total length threshold for the onset of puberty in females, with a critical value established at 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters]. This length is considered the minimum size at which females can successfully undergo gametogenesis, and individuals below this threshold are invariably immature. The relationship between body size and maturity is particularly strong in this species, as reaching the length of 25 centimeters [Lp = 25 centimeters] appears to be a stronger predictor of reproductive readiness than chronological age in many populations. Asymptotic growth, characterized by an ultimate total length of 73 centimeters [Li = 73 centimeters], is achieved only after a prolonged period of post-pubertal growth. These life history parameters together depict a species that delays reproduction until a relatively large body size is attained, thereby maximizing fecundity at first spawning through increased abdominal cavity volume.

Data from long-term monitoring of a subarctic population have yielded estimates of the maximum adult size, with an ultimate wet weight of 10000 grams [Wwi = 10000 grams] recorded for a single, exceptionally old female captured during a gil net survey. This individual likely approached the life span limit of 5475 days [am = 5475 days] estimated for the species, as supported by annular scale ring counts at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. By contrast, the extremely small mass at the yolk-sac larva stage, a wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], appears to be compensated by a high fecundity per spawning event, where individual females may deposit thousands of eggs. The pronounced contrast between the neonatal mass and the ultimate wet weight of 10000 grams [Wwi = 10000 grams] indicates a remarkable growth trajectory spanning several orders of magnitude, sustained by highly efficient food conversion throughout the juvenile and adult stages.
